content: The extracted data from several studies may have been derived from a combination of survey and qualitative data, as the authors did not always specify the source of their findings in the published articles. All studies involving community members and drug distributors as participants were included. Additionally, studies focusing on the perspectives and experiences of mass drug administration (MDA) campaigns for lymphatic filariasis (LF) elimination were considered. Electronic searches were conducted in databases such as the Global Health Library, WHO Global Health Library, Embase (Ovid), MEDLINE (OvidSP), SCOPUS, and Web of Science for eligible studies from 2002 to February 1, 2017. The search strategy was developed by an information specialist, following guidelines from the Cochrane Qualitative Research Methods Group for qualitative evidence synthesis. Keywords and MeSH terms were also drawn from a similar qualitative evidence synthesis. These databases were chosen based on preliminary exploratory searches that suggested they would yield the highest number of relevant results. No restrictions were placed on date, language, or geography. The complete search strategy is detailed in Annex 2. Additional resources were searched, including citation searches of included studies in Google Scholar, SCOPUS, and Web of Science. Key individuals in the field were also asked to submit potentially relevant study titles. Records identified from various sources were compiled into a single EndNote database, and duplicates were removed. Titles and abstracts of the identified records were individually assessed by a reviewer to determine their relevance. Irrelevant references were discarded, and the full texts of relevant papers were retrieved and reviewed for inclusion. Data extraction was performed using a form specifically designed for this synthesis. Key themes and categories relevant to the synthesis objectives were extracted, along with information about the first author, publication date, language, country of study, context (urban or rural), participant group (e.g., infected individuals, relatives, community leaders), theoretical or conceptual framework, and research methods. Data relevant to the systematic review were extracted using a predefined Excel template. Extracted data items included geographical scope, participant age and gender, diagnostic techniques (e.g., blood volume, test type, circulating filarial antigen, IgG4 response to BmR1), markers of LF infection (e.g., disappearance of worm nests visible via ultrasound), drug regimens, drug sources/manufacturers, outcomes, adverse event (AE) definitions and classifications, and descriptions of AE active surveillance approaches. The inclusion criteria required studies to use qualitative methods for both data collection and analysis, constituting a basic quality threshold. Studies not meeting this standard were excluded. To assess methodological quality, a quality appraisal framework was applied to each study, using an adapted version of the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) tool for qualitative studies. This tool included eight questions addressing the adequacy of setting/context descriptions, sampling strategy, data collection strategy, data analysis, evidence supporting claims/findings, reflexivity, sensitivity to ethical concerns, and other concerns. While there is no gold standard for assessing the quality of primary qualitative studies, the adapted CASP checklist was deemed most suitable for this review. A thematic analysis was conducted using the Supporting the Use of Research Evidence (SURE) framework, developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) to assist with evidence-informed policymaking and technical capacity in lowand middle-income countries. This framework has been used in other studies and reviews. The literature database searches yielded 2,458 hits, with an additional 14 references obtained from WHO partners, totaling 2,471 hits. After removing 746 duplicates, 1,725 records were screened for relevance. Discrepancies in relevance assessment between two main reviewers were resolved by an independent expert. Of the 42 relevant articles, 9 were included in the review. Annex 3 lists all evidence sources, and Annex 4 contains the list of 33 excluded studies with reasons for exclusion. The included studies were conducted between 2010 and 2017 and were reported in English. They were located in African, Asian, and Latin American countries, including the Democratic Republic of Congo, Côte d’Ivoire, Haiti, India, Indonesia, Liberia, Malawi, Mali, and Papua New Guinea. Most studies were randomized controlled trials (RCTs), except for a few non-randomized or single-arm studies. Participant ages ranged from 5 years and older, with upper age limits varying from 55 to 80 years. Gender was not considered in the selection or allocation of subjects, except in one study that provided gender-disaggregated data. Sample sizes ranged from 12 to over 10,000 participants, with a median of 102 individuals. Risk of bias (ROB) was assessed using eight criteria. Sequence generation was ranked as low ROB in all studies reporting this feature, except for one study where it was unclear. Allocation concealment was generally unclear or high ROB due to the community-level nature of interventions. Blinding in outcome assessment and data analysis was rarely reported. Reporting bias and disclosure of funding sources or conflicts of interest were either not reported or classified as low ROB. Overall, the quality of evidence was rated as low or very low due to risks of bias and imprecision in estimates. Effectiveness and safety outcomes were analyzed for various drug regimens, including ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine (DEC), and albendazole. Studies comparing these regimens showed significant microfilarial clearance and reduced microfilarial density in intervention arms. However, the quality of evidence was low due to small sample sizes and methodological limitations. Safety data indicated no significant differences in adverse events between intervention and control groups, with wide confidence intervals introducing uncertainty. Further analyses by sub-groups and infection status are detailed in Annex 6.
